correctness.rationale: Assuming \(\mathsf{MC}\), Theorem B of arXiv:2609.20140v2 embeds an arbitrary set into a normal separable algebraic \(L/K\) with \(K\) well-orderable of characteristic \(0\). For every well-orderable intermediate \(F\), characteristic \(0\) persists and \(L/F\) remains normal, separable, and algebraic, so the restricted basis hypothesis supplies exactly the bases required by Theorem A. Theorem A well-orders \(L\), hence the arbitrary set, yielding \(\mathsf{AC}\). The reverse implication follows from \(\mathsf{AC}\). No computation or unproved infinitary extrapolation is used.

evidence: arXiv:2609.20140v2, Corollary 7.1 proves \(\mathsf{AC}\) equivalent to \(\mathsf{MC}\) plus the strictly broader hypothesis that every vector space over every well-orderable characteristic-zero field has a basis.

The source proof of Theorem A, especially its recursive intermediate-field construction, uses bases only for \(L/F\) where \(L/K\) is normal separable algebraic and \(F\) is a well-orderable intermediate field.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The closest broader result is Corollary 7.1. It implies the new restricted hypothesis but does not subsume the new equivalence as a statement about how much of the basis principle is actually necessary; the converse proof verifies the smaller hypothesis suffices.

value.rationale: The restriction isolates a natural Galois-type fragment of the vector-space basis principle that is sufficient, together with multiple choice, to recover full choice without Foundation. This identifies the exact kind of vector spaces used by the new foundation-free well-ordering mechanism and separates that requirement from the much broader “all vector spaces over well-orderable fields” hypothesis.
